newsitem.title: CHINA: Watchful China worries over Hong Kong dissent.
newsitem.headline: Watchful China worries over Hong Kong dissent.

text.p: When hundreds of thousands of protesting students, workers and residents took to the streets of Beijing in 1989, China's communist government hit back with soldiers and tanks.
Dealing with dissent in Hong Kong, which returns to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, may not be so simple.

Beijing officials have been watching with concern the willingness of Hong Kong residents to publicly express political opinions that would land them long terms in jail or detention on the mainland, analysts and diplomats said on Thursday.

Around 55,000 Hong Kong people joined a candle-light vigil on Wednesday night to denounce the Chinese army's June 4, 1989 crackdown against student-led pro-democracy protests centred in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in which hundreds died.
The vigil is an annual tradition that Hong Kong activists have sworn to continue even after the return to China -- and the analysts said Beijing was watching closely.
"There is certainly an interest and concern about continuing political activism after July 1," said one Beijing-based political analyst, who declined to be identified.
"The Chinese will have to confront this," he said.

Beijing was caught between its instinctive desire to ban public dissent and the knowledge that to do so would damage confidence in Hong Kong, which has been promised a high degree of autonomy for 50 years after the handover, diplomats said.
"Everyone is looking to next year and whether Hong Kong people will be allowed to assemble in that way," said one Western diplomat.
"It would be highly inflammatory not to let people gather, but at the same time...how can this system tolerate it?" the diplomat said. "I think it will be a real test."

Hong Kong's Beijing-appointed future leader Tung Chee-hwa has vowed never to create dissident martyrs by allowing a Tiananmen-style crackdown on dissent in the free-wheeling territory, where political protests have long been common.
But Tung has launched plans to trim civil rights, including the right to demonstrate, and has told Hong Kong people to set aside the "baggage of June 4" and focus on the future.
The issue of public protest underlines the gulf between political norms in the People's Republic and those in Hong Kong, which has been ruled as a colony from London for 156 years.

While in Hong Kong tolerance of demonstrations can be seen as the mark of a secure and confident administration, on the mainland -- where memories of the anarchy of the ultra-leftist Cultural Revolution (1966-76) remain vivid -- similar forbearance would be taken as a sign of political weakness.

Despite fears that overt dissent in Hong Kong could spill over into mainland China, Beijing was unlikely to interfere overtly in future demonstrations in the territory for fear of alienating international opinion, the political analyst said.
The confidence of foreign investors is vital for Hong Kong, which has grown rich as a free-trade entrepot, financial centre and a base for multinational companies.

Some Chinese officials were themselves sympathetic to Hong Kong residents' fears for the future, and Beijing was certainly determined to ensure that Hong Kong remained a success, the Western diplomat said.

"The whole world is watching them and they do want to make a good go of this thing," the diplomat said, adding that in the near term, at least, Beijing was unlikely to take tough action in Hong Kong whatever the provocation.
"If the Chinese are going to crack down, it's not going to be this year," she said.

Many Chinese pro-democracy activists and analysts have speculated that the death in February of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who gave the final order for the 1989 crackdown, could open the way for an official re-evaluation of the affair.

Such a rethink could transform the political background to Tiananmen memorial activities, but was unlikely to come in a year that would be dominated by Hong Kong and a major meeting of the Communist Party late in the year, one diplomat said.
"This is the wrong year for it, with the Hong Kong return and the Party Congress," the diplomat said. "Maybe next year."
